title: Stopping distance — thinking and braking
examTip: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Speed affects both, but in different ways. Thinking distance is proportional to speed: double the speed → double the thinking distance. Braking distance is quadratic: double the speed → four times the braking distance. Always explain factors using physics, not just 'it is harder to stop'.
introTips: Stopping distance is one of the most useful topics in GCSE Physics in real life. It directly explains road safety rules like speed limits and drink-driving laws.
Thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed. It is the distance the car travels while the driver takes in the situation and presses the brake.
Braking distance depends on speed (quadratically) and on the grip between the tyres and the road.
Braking transfers the car's kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes. Very heavy braking can make the brakes overheat.
Speed and braking distance have a quadratic relationship. That is why motorway speed limits save so many lives.
intro: Every road safety rule comes from the physics of stopping distance. That includes speed limits, drink-drive limits and the two-second rule. Say something goes wrong ahead of you on a motorway. Your car does not stop the moment your brain spots danger. Your brain takes time to take it in and react. Then your brakes take time to bring the car to a halt. The physics of each stage explains a lot. A tired driver at 70 mph needs far more than twice the road space of an alert driver at 35 mph. It is also why worn tyres and icy roads are so dangerous, even at modest speeds.

keyPoints.heading: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
keyPoints.content: Stopping distance is the total distance a vehicle travels before it stops. It starts when the driver first notices a hazard. It has two separate stages. Thinking distance: the distance travelled while the driver reacts, from seeing the hazard to pressing the brake. Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Braking distance: the distance travelled once the brakes are on, while the car slows to a stop. Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Example values: - at 30 mph: thinking distance ≈ 9 m, braking distance ≈ 14 m, stopping distance ≈ 23 m - at 70 mph: thinking distance ≈ 21 m, braking distance ≈ 75 m, stopping distance ≈ 96 m That is roughly four car-lengths compared with 24 car-lengths.
writeBullets: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
Thinking distance: the distance travelled while the driver reacts (before the brakes are on)
Braking distance: the distance travelled from when the brakes are on until the vehicle stops
Thinking distance = speed × reaction time
Both thinking and braking distance increase with speed

keyTerms.def: Total distance from first noticing a hazard to coming to a complete stop; equals thinking distance + braking distance
Distance travelled during the driver's reaction time before brakes are applied; = speed × reaction time
Distance travelled while the brakes are applied and the vehicle decelerates to rest

keyPoints.memTip: Stop = Think + Brake. Both increase with speed.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to pick out the two stages on a diagram of a car journey from hazard to stop. Also be able to work out thinking distance from speed and reaction time.

keyPoints.heading: Factors affecting reaction time and thinking distance
keyPoints.content: Reaction time is the gap between seeing a hazard and pressing the brake. For an alert driver, it is usually 0.2–0.9 seconds. All of these factors make it longer.

list.definition: slows brain processing significantly — the biggest single impairment
prescription or recreational drugs often impair reaction speed
fatigue slows brain responses; severe tiredness can cause microsleep at the wheel
mobile phone use, adjusting a stereo, or talking to passengers
reaction times tend to slow with age

writeBullets: Typical reaction time: 0.2–0.9 seconds (alert, sober driver)
Alcohol: slows brain processing → longer reaction time → greater thinking distance
Drugs: many impair reaction speed → longer thinking distance
Tiredness: slows brain responses. Severe tiredness can cause microsleep
Distractions (phone, music, conversation): attention is split → hazards are spotted more slowly

keyTerms.def: The time between detecting a hazard and pressing the brake — typically 0.2–0.9 seconds for an alert driver

keyPoints.memTip: ATDS: Alcohol, Tiredness, Drugs, Distractions. All increase reaction time, and so thinking distance.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exam questions often ask 'why does alcohol increase stopping distance?'. Say clearly that it increases reaction time, and so thinking distance. Don't just say 'it slows you down'.

keyPoints.heading: Factors affecting braking distance
keyPoints.content: Several factors affect braking distance. Speed (most important): braking distance is proportional to speed squared. Double the speed → four times the braking distance. This is because kinetic energy = ½mv², and braking distance is proportional to KE. At 30 mph, braking distance ≈ 14 m. At 60 mph it is ≈ 55 m, and at 70 mph ≈ 75 m. Road surface condition: wet or icy roads reduce friction between the tyres and the road. So there is less braking force → longer braking distance. Ice can reduce friction to nearly zero. Tyre condition: worn tyres have less tread → less grip → less braking force → longer braking distance. The UK legal minimum tyre tread depth is 1.6 mm. Brake condition: worn or overheated brakes apply less force. Brake fade (overheated brakes losing their effect) can happen on long downhill stretches.
writeBullets: Speed: braking distance ∝ v². Double the speed → four times the braking distance
Wet or icy roads: less friction between tyres and road → less braking force → longer braking distance
Worn tyres: less tread → reduced grip → less friction → longer braking distance
Worn or overheated brakes: reduced braking force → longer braking distance
All these factors reduce the friction or force available. The car needs more distance to lose the same kinetic energy

keyTerms.def: The force applied by the brakes to decelerate the vehicle; transferred from kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes
The force between tyre and road surface that allows braking — reduced by ice, water, or worn tyres

keyPoints.memTip: Braking distance ∝ v². Double the speed → 4× the distance.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The quadratic link between speed and braking distance catches people out. They often say 'double the distance' for double the speed. It is four times.

keyPoints.heading: Energy analysis of braking
keyPoints.content: When the brakes are on, the car slows down. The kinetic energy of the car is transferred to thermal energy (heat) in the brakes through friction. Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv². KE depends on v². So doubling the speed quadruples the KE. That quadruples the braking distance too, if the braking force stays the same. The brakes, tyres and road surface all heat up during braking. Very heavy braking can make brakes overheat, for example in emergency stops or on long downhill stretches. This makes them less effective. It is called brake fade. Large deceleration = large braking force = KE lost quickly. In emergency braking, the deceleration is very high. Then the forces on passengers are very large. This is why seatbelts and crumple zones are essential. Newton's Second Law: F = ma → braking force = mass × deceleration.
writeBullets: Braking transfers kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes
KE = ½mv². Doubling the speed quadruples the KE, and so the braking distance (at constant braking force)
The brakes, tyres and road all heat up during braking
Brake fade: overheated brakes lose their effect. Dangerous on long descents
F = ma: larger braking force → larger deceleration → shorter stopping distance

keyTerms.def: Energy of a moving object; KE = ½mv²; transferred to thermal energy in brakes during stopping
Reduction in braking effectiveness caused by overheated brakes — a hazard during prolonged or repeated heavy braking

keyPoints.memTip: KE = ½mv². Speed doubles → KE quadruples → braking distance quadruples.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Link back to work and energy: work done by the brakes = KE lost. Braking distance = KE ÷ braking force. This gives the quadratic relationship.

tables.title: Stopping distances at different speeds (standard values)

0.question: A driver has a reaction time of 0.6 s and is travelling at 20 m/s. What is the thinking distance?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 20 × 0.6 = 12 m.
0.wrongFeedback: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 20 m/s × 0.6 s = 12 m. The car travels 12 m before the brakes are even on.

1.question: A car's braking distance at 20 m/s is 25 m. What would the braking distance be at 40 m/s, on the same road?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Braking distance ∝ v². The speed doubles → the distance quadruples: 25 × 4 = 100 m.
1.wrongFeedback: Braking distance is proportional to speed squared. Double the speed → (2)² = 4 times the braking distance: 25 × 4 = 100 m. Not 50 m. It is quadratic, not linear.

3.question: Which energy transfer happens in the brakes as a car stops?
options: Kinetic energy transferred to thermal energy (heat) in the brakes
Potential energy transferred to kinetic energy in the brakes
Thermal energy transferred to kinetic energy in the brakes
Electrical energy transferred to kinetic energy in the brakes
3.correctFeedback: Correct! The brakes apply a friction force that slows the car. Kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy in the brakes, tyres and road surface.
3.wrongFeedback: Braking turns kinetic energy into thermal energy through friction. That is why brakes get hot. They are taking in the car's kinetic energy as heat.

commonMistakes: Saying braking distance doubles when speed doubles. It quadruples, because KE ∝ v². So braking distance ∝ v² at constant braking force.
Mixing up thinking distance and braking distance. Thinking distance is before the brakes are on. Braking distance is after.
Saying alcohol or tiredness increases stopping distance without saying which part. It increases thinking distance (by increasing reaction time), not braking distance.
Forgetting that road and tyre conditions affect braking distance, not thinking distance. Wet roads do not affect reaction time.
Leaving out the energy reasoning when asked why braking distance increases with speed. Always link it to KE = ½mv², which is proportional to v².
examTips: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. It is a one-mark calculation that is easy if you know this formula.
For quadratic relationship questions, say 'braking distance is proportional to speed squared' before the calculation. This earns the explanation mark.
Keep the factors for thinking distance and braking distance separate. Alcohol, tiredness and distractions affect thinking. Road, tyre and brake condition affect braking.
Energy questions: link braking to KE = ½mv² → transferred to thermal energy in the brakes. This explains why faster cars need more braking distance.
